items.text: In this lesson you meet a new neighbour. You say where you are from and spell your name. You ask questions with do and does. Then you read a library form and fill in your own.

In this lesson you meet a new neighbour. Samir is new in Park Road. He meets Lena. She lives next door. They say hello and ask two questions. Where are you from? Do you work near here? Lena writes Samir's name in her phone. She asks: How do you spell it? Samir says the letters, one at a time. S-A-M-I-R.

First, am, is and are. I am. He is. She is. You are. We are. They are. Often we say the short form: I'm from Egypt. She's a nurse. Then, questions with do and does. With I, you, we and they, say do. Do you work here? Yes, I do. No, I don't. With he and she, say does. Does she work here? Yes, she does. No, she doesn't. After does, the verb has no s. Where does he live?

Next, you read a form for a library card. A form asks for your details. Your first name, your surname, your address and your postcode. Many forms say: write in capital letters. Capital letters are easy to read. Then you read an appointment card. Look for the day, the time and what to bring. Last, you write about yourself and fill in a form.

Then you join a library. The person at the desk asks questions. What's your first name? And your surname? Spell your name slowly and clearly. Y-U-S-U-F. Say your date of birth, your address and your postcode. When the question starts with do, give a short answer. Yes, I do. No, I don't.
Last, you read a short story about a person in a new town. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you talk about your family and the people you know. You say who people are and what they are like. You read about the people on a street. Then you describe a person at a station.

In this lesson you talk about the people in your life. Ana shows her colleague Omar a family photo. Omar asks: Who's this? And: What's she like? What's she like? asks about the person. Is she kind? Is she funny? Ana answers: That's my uncle. He's tall and kind. Listen for the family words: parents, grandmother, uncle and cousins.

Before a person or a thing, say my, your, his, her or their. For a man, say his: his name. For a woman, say her: her name. For two people, say their: their house. To say whose, add 's to a name: Ana's uncle, my mother's brother. To describe a person, use is or has. She's tall. He has short hair and glasses. Two describing words? Put and between them. He's tall and kind.

Next, you read about the people on Kwame's street. There are neighbours, a colleague, a boss, a cat and a dog. Read it once. Then read it again, slowly, for the details. Then you write about a person you know. Say who they are, what they look like and what they are like.

Then you meet someone at a station. But where is she? A station assistant helps you. Describe the person clearly. She's short. She has grey hair and glasses. She has a red coat. The assistant asks questions. Answer with she and her. When the assistant finds her, say thank you.
Last, you read a short story about the people in a family. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you talk about homes. You ask about a flat on the phone and say where things are. You read an advert for a flat. Then you describe a room so a friend could draw it.

In this lesson you talk about homes. Carlos needs a flat. He sees an advert, and he phones the landlord. He asks: How many rooms are there? Is there a washing machine? Where is the flat? Listen for the answers. The rent is 750 pounds a month. The flat is on the second floor.

To say what is in a place, use there is and there are. One thing: there's a shower. Two or more: there are three rooms. To ask, put is first. Is there a bath? No, there isn't. To say where things are, use in, on, next to, behind and between. The washing machine is in the kitchen, next to the fridge. Between needs two things: between the bed and the window.

Next, you read an advert for a flat. Look for the rent, the floor and the rooms. What is in each room? Then you describe a room in your home. Say what is in it and where. Give numbers too: one window, two shelves. Write it so a friend could draw the room.

Then you phone about the flat in the advert. First, say why you are calling. I'm calling about the flat on Green Lane. Ask five questions. Is there a washing machine? Is there a bus stop near the flat? Last, describe your own home. How many rooms are there? What is in them?
Last, you read a short story about a home. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you are in an English class. You ask for help. You say what you can do and what you like doing. You read a course timetable and write a short note. Then you enrol on a course.

In this lesson you are in an English class. The teacher speaks, and Mei doesn't understand. That's OK. She asks for help. She says: Sorry, can you say that again, please? She asks about a new word: What does free time mean? And she asks: How do you spell dancing? Asking is good. It helps you learn.

To say what you can do, use can and a verb. I can swim. I can dance. The verb after can has no to and no s. She can drive. For no, say can't. I can't drive. Listen: can is short and quiet, and can't is long and strong. To say what you like doing, use like and a verb with -ing. I like cooking. I love dancing.

Next, you read a course timetable. Look for the days, the times, the rooms and the levels. Then you write a short note to your teacher. Start every sentence with a capital letter. End it with a full stop or a question mark. Names and days have capital letters too: Monday, Ms Clarke.

Then you enrol on an English course. Say: I'd like to enrol on an English course, please. Ask about the days, the times and the level. Say what you can do. I can read a little, but I can't write well. You don't understand? Say: Can you say that again, please?
Last, you read a short story about learning something new. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you go to a market and buy fruit and vegetables. You ask the prices, choose what you want and pay. Then you read a price list and a receipt. You check your change.

In this lesson you buy food at a market. At a market, people sell fruit and vegetables at a stall. First, you ask the price. How much are these apples? How much is this bag? Then you ask for what you want. Can I have a kilo, please? To choose one thing, you can point and say: That one, please. The big one. Listen carefully to the numbers. Thirteen and thirty sound close. If you are not sure, ask: Sorry, thirteen or thirty?

Now, numbers up to a thousand. After hundred, say and. Two hundred and fifty. Three hundred and twenty-five. Say a price like this: four pounds seventy, or just four seventy. For pence, people often say p. Eighty p is eighty pence. Next, this, that, these and those. This and these are near you. That and those are not near you. This bag, these apples. That bag, those apples. You don't need to say the thing again. Say one or ones. The big one. The green ones.

Next, you read a price list and a receipt from a market stall. The price list shows the price for a kilo, or for one thing. The receipt shows what you bought, the total and your change. Look at the receipt and the price list together. Is every price the same? Then you write your own shopping list, with an amount for every thing.

Then you buy three things at a stall. Ask the prices, and say how much you want. Ask for a receipt, and check it before you go. Is something not right? Say it politely: Sorry, I think there's a mistake.
Last, you read a short story about money and shopping. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you talk about your day and your week. You say what time you do things and how often you do them. You also read a shift rota. Then you find a time to meet a friend.

In this lesson you talk about your day and your week. First, two colleagues talk on a break at work. They ask: What do you do on Saturdays? What time do you get up? They also ask: How often do you see her? The answer is: Every Saturday. Listen for the days of the week, and for the times. Listen to the end of the verbs too: she works, he watches.

Now the grammar. For your routine, use the present simple. I work. You work. We work. They work. But with he and she, add s. She works. He starts at two. After ch and sh, add es. He watches. In this lesson you buy food at a stall, and you cook. You ask for amounts: a kilo of rice, a tin of tomatoes. Then you read a recipe. You also explain how to make a dish you know.

In this lesson you buy food, and you cook. First, Kwame buys food at a stall in the market. Listen for the amounts: a kilo of rice, a packet of butter, two tins of tomatoes. The stallholder asks: Anything else? Kwame says what he wants: I'll have a piece, please. When you have everything, say: That's all, thanks.

Now two grammar points. One: you can count apples and eggs. An apple, two eggs. You can't count rice, butter or cheese. Say some rice, some butter. To count them, say a packet of rice, a piece of cheese, two tins of soup. Two: instructions. An instruction starts with the verb. Cut the onions. Add the rice. Put the steps in order with first, then, after that and finally.

Next, you read the back of a packet of rice. The label tells you how to cook the rice and where to keep it. The recipe has two parts: what you need, and what to do. Read what you need first. Then follow the steps in order. After that, you write a recipe for a dish you know.

In this lesson you are ill and you need help. You say what is wrong at a chemist, you phone a clinic to make an appointment, and you read a medicine label so you know how much to take.

In this lesson you are ill, and you need help. First, you go to a chemist. A chemist sells medicine and gives advice. You do not need an appointment. The chemist asks: What's the matter? You say what is wrong. At the end, people often say: I hope you feel better soon.

There are three ways to say what is wrong. One: I've got, and the problem. I've got a headache. I've got a cough. Two: my, the part of your body, and hurts. My back hurts. My throat hurts. Three: I feel, and how you feel. I feel ill. I feel tired. To give advice, use should. You should rest. You should see a doctor. Do not say should to. Say: you should rest.

Next, you read a medicine label. A label answers four questions. How much? How often? How much in one day? And what must you not do? Read it slowly. The numbers are important. Then you write a short note for the doctor: what is wrong, when it started, and one question.

Then you phone a clinic and make an appointment. Say: I'd like to make an appointment, please. The receptionist asks your name, your problem and a time. Say the time back to check it: Four o'clock? Yes, that's fine.
Last, you read a short story about a visit to the doctor. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you buy clothes. You compare prices and sizes, and you try things on. Then you read a returns notice. You also take something back to a shop.

In this lesson you buy clothes, and you take something back. First, Samir buys a jacket for his new job. The shop assistant asks: Which one do you want? Samir asks: Have you got it in blue? Can I try it on? Then he says what is wrong: It's too small. Listen to how some words join: Can I try it on? Have you got it in blue?

Now the grammar. To compare two things, add er and say than. The grey jacket is cheaper than the black one. With long words, say more: more expensive. For three or more things, say the cheapest, or the most expensive. Good and bad are different: better, the best. Worse, the worst. To say something is not right, use too or enough. Too goes before the word: too small. Enough goes after it: not long enough.

Next, you read a notice in a clothes shop. It is about returns and exchanges. When can you take clothes back? What must you bring? Then you write an email to a shop. Start with Dear, and say what the problem is.

Then you take something back to a shop. Say what you bought and when. Say the problem: They're too small. Ask for another size: Can I exchange them for a larger size? Is there no other size? Then ask: Can I have my money back?

In this lesson you are out in town. You ask the way, follow directions and read signs. At the end, you tell a visitor the way to your home.

In this lesson you are out in town. You need to find a place. First, you listen to Samir. He has a job interview at the museum. But he doesn't know the way. He stops a woman in the street. He says: Excuse me. Could you tell me the way to the museum, please? Could you is very polite. It is good with people you don't know. Listen to Samir. He asks the woman to say it again. Then he says the directions back. This is a good habit. It helps you remember the way.

Directions start with a verb. Go straight on. Turn left. Go past the cinema. Cross the bridge. Turn left tells you where to go. On the left tells you where the place is. Turn left at the bank. The café is on the left. At the end, say where the place is. Use opposite, between, in front of or behind. The museum is opposite the park. The post office is between the bank and the café. Do not say opposite of. Say: opposite the park. But say: in front of the cinema.

Next, you read a notice. Its title is How to find us. It tells visitors the way from the station to a community centre. On the way, there is a sign on a bridge. The bridge is closed, so you need a new way. Read the dates and the numbers slowly. They are important. Then you write directions from the station to your home. Write one step on each line.

In the task, a colleague is coming to your home. She is at the station, and she phones you. Tell her the way, one step at a time. Name things she can see: the traffic lights, a supermarket, a park. Then you change roles. Your teacher gives you directions to a new place. Say them back to check.

In this lesson you talk about now and about last weekend. You read a story and a form about a lost bag. Then you say sorry because you missed a party.

In this lesson you talk about now, and about last weekend. First, you listen to two colleagues, Carlos and Mei. It is Monday morning, in the office kitchen. Mei asks: What are you doing? Carlos says: I'm making coffee. That is about now. Then Mei asks: How was your weekend? What did you do? That is about the past. Listen to the end of the past verbs. Worked ends in a t sound. Played ends in a d sound. Visited has one more part: vis-it-ed.

For now, use am, is or are, and a verb with -ing. I'm cooking. She's working. What are you doing? For the past, most verbs add -ed. I worked. We played football. I visited my aunt. Some verbs change. Go is went. Have is had. See is saw. To ask about the past, use did. Did you go out? What did you do? After did, the verb does not change. Say: Did you go? Not: Did you went?

Next, you read a short story, The green bag. Amina is late, and she leaves her bag on the bus. Then you read a form for lost things. It says what she lost, when and where. Then you write a message to say why you were late. Say sorry, and say what happened.

This is the last lesson of Level 1. You buy a train ticket and plan a day by the sea. You also read a departures board and give reasons for your plans.

This is the last lesson of Level 1. You travel by train, and you make plans. First, you listen to Tomasz at the ticket desk. He wants to go to the sea tomorrow. The clerk asks: Single or return? A single takes you there. A return takes you there and back. Tomasz asks: What time does the first train leave? Listen for the time and the platform. Then he meets his colleague Ana. She asks: Shall we go together? That is an idea for two people.

To ask for something, say Can I…? Can I have a window seat, please? To offer to do something, say I'll and a verb. I'll wait for you. I'll buy the tickets. I'll is I will. Say it as one short word. To give a reason, use because and a sentence. I need a day at the beach because work is busy. Or use to and a verb. I'll come early to buy coffee. After to, the verb does not change.

Next, you read a departures board at a station. It shows the time, the place and the platform of each train. Look at the end of each line. Is the train on time, delayed or cancelled? Then you read a ticket. Find the date, the seat and the last train back. Last, you write a text to a friend with a plan. Give one or two reasons.

Last, you read a short story about a day out. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions. After this lesson comes the A1 review and check. Then you start Level 2.
